endorsements.quote: In the context of LLMs in clinical practice, this requires the patient to be informed that LLMs might be used by the medical practitioners that are providing patient care, such that the consent that the patient provides to receive that care can be adequately informed (the WHO 2021 guidance states that ‘the use of machine‐learning algorithms [such as LLMs] in diagnosis, prognosis and treatment plans should be incorporated into the process for informed and valid consent’) [ 31 ].

The patient must understand, retain, weight up, and communicate back to the medical practitioner this information in order for the consent that they provide to receive medical care that is influenced by LLMs to be informed.

This requires medical practitioners to explain the manner in which LLMs will be deployed in their care (specifically, that LLMs will be deployed by the medical practitioner as tools in the delivery of patient care, rather than those practitioners delegating or entirely handing over clinical decision‐making responsibilities to these technologies), the reasons of beneficence for doing so, and the potential threats to non‐maleficence that they pose.

unlisted_practices: Medical practitioners must provide care without LLM augmentation for patients who do not consent to LLM involvement.
Use LLMs as tools that support clinicians rather than delegating clinical decision-making responsibility to them.
Do not deploy LLMs in clinical care unless risks of patient harm are sufficiently mitigated through reliable quality control regulations.

screen.reason: This is an ethical analysis/commentary paper evaluating the implications of LLMs in clinical practice using the principlism framework and proposing recommendations around patient consent and risk mitigation.
